title: Beethoven: the exposition reshaped
question: What changes when the second tune returns in C major?
intro: The opening returns in C minor; the second tune returns in C major instead of E♭ major, and its horn call moves to bassoons. The oboe gains a solo. This comparison stops before the coda at bar 374. Timing is aligned automatically, not checked by ear.

scoreChanges.text: The first violins move G–G–G–E♭ up an octave, from G4–E♭4 to G5–E♭5. An F on the first quaver of bar 248 replaces the opening rest. Flutes and oboes, silent in bars 1–5, now add harmony around the returning C-minor theme.

The oboe gains a line beginning on C, and the cellos replace their held C with a plucked C an octave lower. First violins add A♭–A♭–A♭ then G before the familiar entries. Their C in bar 256 lasts one beat rather than the three beats tied across bars 9–10.

An Adagio oboe solo is inserted into the pause corresponding to bar 21: after a held G come F–E♭–D, a quick E♭–D–C–D turn, then F–E♭–D with another pause. The whole unmeasured addition belongs to bar 268. It lengthens a paired bar; it does not create extra numbered bars or establish a slower tempo.

The three-bar fortissimo A♭–F statement in bars 22–24, ending in a written pause, is omitted. After the oboe solo, bar 269 goes directly to the piano A♭–A♭–A♭ figure corresponding to bar 25. The transition is three numbered bars shorter, despite the added solo.

The first violins’ F held across bars 30–32 becomes moving quavers in bars 274–276: F–D–D–D, B–A♭–A♭–A♭, then G–B–B–B. Their next bar begins on C instead of the E♭ in bar 33. This is a rewritten passage, not a faster performance of the held note.

The cellos now join the descending quavers instead of repeating C beneath them. The first violins’ G♭ in bar 54 is respelled F♯ in bar 298. The transition’s final chord changes from B♭–D–F in bar 58, preparing E♭ major, to G–B–D in bar 302, preparing C major.

The horns’ call sounds B♭–B♭–B♭–E♭–F–B♭ in bars 59–62. Bassoons take it over in bars 303–306 as G–G–G–C–D–G, a minor third lower, retaining its short repeated notes and longer following notes. The horns no longer introduce the call; they enter on the sustained G at bar 306.

The four-bar violin tune B♭–E♭–D–E♭–F–C–C–B♭ becomes G–C–B–C–D–A–A–G: C major replaces E♭ major. Its next statement passes to flute and oboes in bars 311–314, where both violin parts rest; bars 67–70 instead give the melody to clarinet with second-violin accompaniment.

Bars 319–322 add another four-bar statement of the C-major tune in the flute, with oboe and bassoon harmony. Both violin parts rest. This extra statement has no separate counterpart between exposition bars 74 and 75.

The violin phrase B♭–C–D♭–C is retained, but its next two bars pass to flute and clarinet as B♭–C–B♭–A, replacing A♭ with A♮. The next violin phrase, D♭–E♭–F–E♭ in bars 79–80, becomes C–D–E♭–D in bars 327–328, followed by another woodwind answer.

The build before the closing group grows from eleven bars, 83–93, to fifteen, 331–345. The strings’ E♭–F–G♭–F pattern becomes F–G–A♭–G. Later the return introduces F♯–G and A–G, while the bassoons sustain D instead of the exposition’s closing repeated Cs.

The pairing shows bars 339–342 as the four extra bars within that rewritten build: first violins alternate F♯–G and A–G over bassoon D. It then pairs the final three-bar approaches, 91–93 and 343–345. This is an editorial correspondence between changed phrases, not a claim that the added bars are a literal copy.

The closing group now supports C major. First violins begin on B♭ in octaves at bar 94, but on a single G at bar 346. The descending passage includes G–F–E–D–C instead of B♭–A♭–G–F–E♭: E♮ is now the third of the home-key major chord.

The exposition ends with an E♭–G–B♭ chord in bar 122 and two bars of rest before the repeat. There is no separate matching three-bar ending before the coda: the next C-major arrival, bar 374, also begins the coda and lies outside this comparison.

listenFor: Compare the horn and bassoon calls and the added oboe solo, keeping changes of key, scoring and written length separate from the build’s provisional duration and relative-level measurements.

sources.title: Mutopia 941: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, first movement — Breitkopf and Härtel, 1862–65, encoded by Stelios Samelis and adapted by Johannes Heinecke
